Bolled
BOLD
adjective
From boll, the rounded seed-pod or capsule of a plant (Old English bolla, “a bowl, a rounded vessel”); hence bolled, “podded, gone to seed-vessel” — the flax standing in bud, and so near to its ripening.

Biblical Definition

Bolled means podded — formed into the boll, the rounded seed-vessel of the flax, as a bowl is a rounded thing; the two words are one. To say the flax was bolled is to say it stood in bud, its capsules formed, within a few weeks of harvest. The word occurs once in all Scripture, and it occurs as a date: “And the flax and the barley was smitten: for the barley was in the ear, and the flax was bolled” (Exo 9:31). The seventh plague fell upon a growing field, and Moses tells us exactly what stage the crops had reached — barley in the ear, flax in the boll — and then tells us what the hail spared: “But the wheat and the rie were not smitten: for they were not grown up” (Exo 9:32). Barley and flax head early; wheat and spelt head late. That is a particular few weeks of the Egyptian year, and the record is precise enough to be laid against the growing season of the Nile. The Holy Ghost did not have to say this. He said it because the plagues were not a parable but an event — in a real month, on a real crop, in a real country — and the hail smote “throughout all the land of Egypt all that was in the field” (Exo 9:25), while “only in the land of Goshen, where the children of Israel were, was there no hail” (Exo 9:26). The judgment was datable, and the mercy was addressed.

Webster 1828 Definition

Podded; formed into the boll, the rounded seed-vessel — said of the flax standing in bud, near its ripening.

BOLLED, podded; swollen into the boll, the rounded seed-vessel of a plant.

From boll, Old English bolla, “a bowl, a rounded vessel.”

Of the flax it means in bud, the capsules formed, and near to harvest.

A KJV hapax, occurring but once (Exo 9:31).

It fixes the season of the seventh plague: barley in the ear, flax in the boll.

Key Scripture

Exo 9:31 — "And the flax and the barley was smitten: for the barley was in the ear, and the flax was bolled."

Exo 9:32 — "But the wheat and the rie were not smitten: for they were not grown up."

Exo 9:25 — "And the hail smote throughout all the land of Egypt all that was in the field, both man and beast; and the hail smote every herb of the field, and brake every tree of the field."

Exo 9:26 — "Only in the land of Goshen, where the children of Israel were, was there no hail."

Modern Corruption

Not a contested doctrine but an old word for podded; it recovers that the plagues fell upon a datable harvest — history, and not parable.

expand to see more

The word rebukes the habit of reading the Exodus as a story about God rather than an account of what God did. One participle fixes the calendar: the flax was bolled and the barley was in the ear, while the wheat and the rie were not grown up. Barley and flax head early in Egypt, and wheat and spelt head late; that is a particular few weeks of a particular year, and Moses states it because he was there and saw it. Scripture does not date a fable. The hail fell upon a field a man could have walked out into and counted the broken stalks, and the God who sent it acts in months and mornings, not in edifying ideas.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word itself, and the plague it dates is plain history. The principle to recover is that the judgment was addressed. The hail smote throughout all the land of Egypt all that was in the field, both man and beast, and brake every tree of the field — and “only in the land of Goshen, where the children of Israel were, was there no hail.” The same storm that ruined the flax of Egypt did not bruise a boll in Goshen. The wrath of God is not weather: it falls where He sends it and it stops where He says. The bolled flax of Egypt and the untouched flax of Goshen, under one sky in one hour, preach the discriminating mercy that shelters His own in the day of His anger.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means podded — formed into the boll, the rounded seed-vessel of a plant.

Bolled — from boll, the rounded seed-pod or capsule of a plant.

From the Old English bolla, “a bowl, a rounded vessel.”

Of the flax it means in bud, the capsules formed, near ripening.

A KJV hapax: the flax was bolled when the hail fell (Exo 9:31).

It dates the seventh plague: barley in the ear, wheat not yet grown up.

Usage

"The barley was in the ear, and the flax was bolled — the hail fell on a datable field."

"Bolled is kin to bowl: the flax had rounded into its seed-vessels and stood near harvest."

"The wheat and the rie were not grown up, and were spared: the plague was precise to the crop."
